label: Slow ops by namespace (Orders.Create)
rule: Red: incident p95 is at least 30% and at least 100 ms worse than reference. 191 ms vs 41 ms is +366% and +150 ms.

why.summary: Orders.Create operations stayed well under slowms in the reference hour, then ran long and queued during the incident hour.
steps: Profiler/slow-log groups ops past slowms by namespace; Orders.Create keeps a steady backlog.
p95 rises through the hour and is still climbing at 10:00, so this is a sustained queue, not one spike.
Same namespace and same API as the report, so this slow-op row is the primary confirmation.
why.dataNote: Slow ops come from periodic profiler samples, so counts are a sample of activity, not a full capture.

label: WiredTiger read/write tickets
rule: Red: tickets out is at least 30% and at least 25 tickets worse than reference. 126 vs 25 of 128 is +404% and +101 tickets.

why.summary: WiredTiger's concurrent transaction tickets were almost all in use, so operations queued for a free ticket instead of running.
steps: serverStatus.wiredTiger.concurrentTransactions shows 126 of 128 tickets out during the incident.
With only 2 tickets left, new reads and writes wait, which shows up as rising slow ops.
Ticket pressure is near the ceiling for the whole hour, so this is exhaustion, not a transient peak.
why.dataNote: Ticket counts are point-in-time snapshots sampled every minute, so short sub-minute peaks can be missed.

label: Replication lag
rule: Red: lag is at least 30% and at least 5 s worse than reference (5 s replaces the 100 ms unit). 22 s vs 1.3 s is +1592% and +20.7 s.

why.summary: The secondary fell tens of seconds behind the primary and the oplog window shrank, so reads served from it were stale.
steps: replSetGetStatus shows per-member lag growing from about 1 s to over 20 s across the hour.
The oplog window dropped from about 48 h to 6 h, so the replica was applying slower than the primary wrote.
Lag was still high at 10:00, which matches a sustained write backlog, not a brief blip.
why.dataNote: Lag is sampled from replSetGetStatus every minute; the true peak between samples can be higher.

label: WiredTiger cache pressure
rule: Amber: cache used is at least 15% and at least 10 percentage points worse than reference (10 pp replaces the 100 ms unit). 74% vs 61.5% is +20% and +12.5 pp.

why.summary: The cache moved well into the pressure zone and eviction more than doubled, but it did not reach the max and dirty pages stayed low.
steps: serverStatus.wiredTiger.cache shows used bytes rising from about 61% to 74% of max.
Eviction rose from about 900 to 2600 pages per minute, so some reads missed cache and went to disk.
Cache stayed under max and did not force application threads to evict, which is why this is amber, not red.
why.dataNote: Cache gauges are sampled each minute; the eviction rate is a delta between samples.

label: Connection count
rule: Amber: current connections is at least 15% and at least 20 connections worse than reference (20 replaces the 100 ms unit). 149 vs 120 is +24% and +29 connections.

why.summary: More clients connected during the incident and totalCreated rose, but the pool still had plenty of available connections.
steps: serverStatus.connections shows current rising from about 120 to 149 of a 700 limit.
available stayed above 550, so the pool never ran out; connecting clients just took slots.
There is real headroom left, so this is a warning, not exhaustion.
why.dataNote: Connection counts are sampled each minute; churn between samples is not visible.

label: Global lock write queue
rule: Amber: queued writers is at least 15% and at least 2 ops worse than reference (2 replaces the 100 ms unit). 3.7 vs 0.4 is +825% and +3.3, above watch, below the 5-op red line.

why.summary: A small but steady queue of writers built up behind the global lock, without reaching the level of a hard stall.
steps: serverStatus.globalLock.currentQueue shows writers queued rising from near zero to around four.
Readers queued moved a little, so the pressure is mostly on writes.
The queue stays modest and no writer waits long enough to be red, so this is a watch.
why.dataNote: Queue depth is sampled each minute; the true peak between samples can be higher.

label: Slow ops by namespace (Orders.Create)
rule: Green: incident p95 is neither 30%+ nor 100 ms worse than reference. 44 ms vs 41 ms is +7% and +3 ms.

why.summary: Orders.Create operation latency was flat across both hours, so slow ops do not explain the reported slowdown.
steps: p95 moved from 41 ms to 44 ms, within normal minute-to-minute noise.
Slow ops per minute stayed in single digits.
This row rules the namespace out rather than pointing at it.
why.dataNote: Slow ops come from periodic profiler samples, so counts are a sample of activity, not a full capture.

label: WiredTiger read/write tickets
rule: Green: tickets out is neither 30%+ nor 25 tickets worse than reference. 26.5 vs 25 of 128 is +6% and +1.5 tickets.

why.summary: Plenty of WiredTiger tickets stayed free, so operations never queued for one.
steps: Tickets out stayed around 26 of 128 for both hours.
More than 100 tickets were available at all times.
Ticket contention is not part of the slowdown.
why.dataNote: Ticket counts are point-in-time snapshots sampled every minute.

label: Replication lag
rule: Green: lag is neither 30%+ nor 5 s worse than reference. 1.3 s vs 1.2 s is +8% and +0.1 s.

why.summary: The replica kept up with the primary through the incident hour and the oplog window stayed wide.
steps: replSetGetStatus lag stayed at about one second, bouncing between 1 and 2.
The oplog window was roughly 48 hours in both windows.
Replication is not the cause of the reported slowdown.
why.dataNote: Lag is sampled from replSetGetStatus every minute.

label: Collection scans (COLLSCAN)
rule: Gray: not collected. Needs the database profiler turned on (profiling level 0 is the default), which this deployment does not run.

why.summary: No collection-scan numbers are shown because the profiler was off for the whole window.
steps: COLLSCAN counts come from system.profile, which only fills when profiling is enabled.
Profiling level here is 0 (off), so nothing was written for 08:00 to 10:00.
This is absent data, not evidence that no scans happened.
why.dataNote: To collect this, enable the profiler (or sample with a slowms threshold) before the next occurrence.

label: Index usage (IXSCAN vs COLLSCAN)
rule: Gray: not collected. Needs profiler output or the $indexStats privilege, neither of which is granted to this read-only collector.

why.summary: Index-usage numbers are missing because the collector cannot read profiler output or $indexStats on this deployment.
steps: Index activity is derived from system.profile or the $indexStats aggregation.
The read-only role does not hold that privilege and the profiler is off.
So the window was never sampled; the row is blank, not green.
why.dataNote: Grant $indexStats (or enable sampling) and this row can be filled next time.

label: Oplog window
rule: Gray: not collected. Needs the clusterMonitor role (or local-database read) to run rs.printReplicationInfo, which is not granted here.

why.summary: The oplog window is not shown because the collector has no permission to read it on this deployment.
steps: rs.printReplicationInfo requires clusterMonitor or access to the local database.
The read-only account here has neither, so the command was never run.
Missing permission means no sample, so the state is gray rather than green.
why.dataNote: Replication *lag* may still appear on its own row if replSetGetStatus is permitted; only the oplog-window row is blind here.
